newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's new top cop no stranger to controversy.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's new top cop no stranger to controversy.

text.p: Mexico's new Attorney General Jorge Madrazo Cuellar is an independent human rights lawyer who is no stranger to controversy or sudden call-ups to government hot seats.
A law professor at Mexico's National Autonomous University, Madrazo was until Monday the head of the government Human Rights Commission.
He took that job in 1993 after the Commission's founding president Jorge Carpizo took over the attorney general's position, which Madrazo himself now holds.
In 1994 he was appointed government peace envoy to Zapatista rebels in the southern state of Chiapas after the sudden resignation of Manuel Camacho Solis, the original envoy.
He held that position for several months at a time of tense relations between the rebels and the government of then President Carlos Salinas de Gortari.

Though he achieved little progress towards a peace accord before returning to the Human Rights Commission, Madrazo -- who does not belong to any political party -- made a blistering attack on the social inequities in Chiapas before leaving the job.
On Monday he took over as attorney general after the firing of Antonio Lozano Gracia for bungling a series of high-profile political murder investigations.
Madrazo, 43, is generally respected for his human rights work but has not been immune to criticism.

At the outbreak of the Zapatista rebellion in January 1994, his Human Rights Commission was accused by other human rights groups of playing down the Mexican army's involvement in summary executions of rebels and the torture and forced disappearance of Chiapas peasants.
"The National Human Rights Commission was complicit in covering up" three such cases, the U.S.-based Americas Watch group said in a 1994 report.
However, it also said that the Salinas government had "impeded the Commission from fully or impartially disclosing its findings in sensitive cases."
